headline: Bass gone to the night shift — porgies picking up the slack out front
subhead: Daytime stripers have quit the reefs, but scup, bluefish, and a few night-tide bass are keeping rods bent from Mattituck to the Gut.
body_markdown:
Kid pulled up to the ramp at Mattituck Inlet Tuesday morning, maybe six-thirty, and he had that look — the one where a fella's spent three hours working a rip he caught fish in back in June and got nothing for it but a sunburn. He asked me straight out, "Pat, where'd the bass go?" I told him the same thing I've been telling fellas at that ramp for sixty summers when the water gets like this. They didn't go anywhere. They just quit working days.

That's the truth of it right now. Sound surface is sitting in the low-to-mid 70s — Kings Point's reading just under 71, New London's holding around 69 and change, and that's enough heat to push the stripers down onto structure and current seams where it's cooler, and to shut their daytime feeding off almost entirely. I've seen this pattern more summers than I care to count. When the water gets up into that range, the bass don't disappear, they just go nocturnal on you. Come dusk they climb back up onto the rock piles off Horton Point and Rocky Point and they'll eat — eels fished slow along bottom, bunker chunks soaking on a fish-finder rig in the current seams where the reef drops into deeper water. Last few nights the guys fishing the two hours either side of the tide change off Horton have done best, mostly schoolies with a few better fish mixed in, nothing to write home about size-wise but a real bite if you're willing to be out there when it's dark and the mosquitoes are working you over.

Daytime, if you want bass, you're fishing deep and slow over structure and hoping. I wouldn't build a trip around it. What I would build a trip around right now is porgies, because that bite hasn't missed a beat all month. The scup are thick around the rock structure and reef edges from Mattituck straight through to the Orient side, and they don't care one bit that the surface water's warm — they're down on bottom where it's cooler and the current keeps bait moving past them. Hi-lo rig, two hooks, squid strips or a piece of clam, small enough hooks that you're not feeding them a mouthful they can't handle. Anchor up tight to the rock piles, not right on top, and let the current bring the smell to them. Some real dinner-plate fish coming over the rail this week, not just the pan-size stuff.

Fluke have softened up some in the shallower water, same story as everywhere else on the Sound this time of year — they've slid off the open flats and into the deeper channel bends and the mouths where there's still cool water moving. Mattituck Inlet itself has been the more consistent producer, working the channel edges on the last of the ebb with a bucktail and a Gulp strip, white or chartreuse, dragged slow along bottom. Plum Gut approach has given up a few better fish too for the boats willing to work the deeper edges where the current cuts hard, but you need to time it right — that current there doesn't forgive a sloppy drift.

Bluefish are still the most reliable thing to actually see happening on the water. Bunker pods have been pushing through past Rocky Point and around the inlet mouth at first light, and when the blues get under them it's the real thing — surface busting up, gulls working it over, blues in the three-to-six-pound range hitting anything shiny you throw at them. Poppers, metal, doesn't much matter, just get it in front of them before the school moves off, because they don't sit still long. Weakfish have been mixed in here and there on the same tides the bass are working at night, nothing you can plan a trip around, but a nice surprise on a bunker chunk if one finds your bait.

Moon's building toward full in the first days of August, and that means the current through the Gut and the Race is going to sharpen up as we go. That's worth watching close. Every year about this time, once that current gets some real push behind it, bait starts stacking against the structure out there and you get your first hints of something different showing up — I'm not going to promise anything's arrived yet because nothing has, but Plum Gut and Orient Point are exactly where I'd be keeping one eye open over the next week or two as that tide builds. In the meantime, fish the porgies with confidence, work the bass after dark if you've got the patience for it, and don't waste your good daylight hours pounding water that's already told you it's not going to give up a striper before the sun goes down.
